content.title: Official Answer to Reviewer pxRk
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback and comments. Below we address your concerns:

**1- The literature review is not enough. (1) There are many previous works that discussed latent action space, action abstraction, etc. But this paper only considers LASER.**

Thanks for pointing that out. In our previous related work section, we discussed methods for action abstraction that either construct action abstraction based on classical robotics control theory or learn such representations via self-supervised learning, LASER being only one of them. We chose to only survey methods that are directly relevant to our scope. However, we have now extended the section to include more action representation learning methods.

**2- A line of works named Modular RL that solves robot control with MARL is totally ignored by this paper. E.g. One Policy to Control Them All:Shared Modular Policies for Agent-Agnostic Control, My Body is a Cage: the Role of Morphology in Graph-Based Incompatible Control, METAMORPH: LEARNING UNIVERSAL CONTROLLERS WITH TRANSFORMERS, STRUCTURE-AWARE TRANSFORMER POLICY FOR INHOMOGENEOUS MULTI-TASK REINFORCEMENT LEARNING.**

The list of papers you mention deals with multi-task reinforcement learning and not multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). While the two fields are related on a very high level, they are fundamentally different. Our work is concerned with the latter.

**3- The proposed method is not sound enough. This work is built upon Dec-POMDP. However, for robot control, there is no need to use partial observations, because these robots are very close to each other.**

The reason we choose DEC-POMDPs is to avoid the curse of dimensionality. When the number of robots grows the state and action space naturally grow to a point where learning/exploration becomes very challenging and expensive, having separate agents handle a sub-part of the observation reduces this burden. In addition, the choice of DEC-POMDPs makes it possible to reuse components in the event that a robot is added or replaced in a new task within the same environment.

Nonetheless, as you can see in section 3.2. Our approach is also fit for the case where the different agents share the same observation (figure 2). We ran additional experiments where our method as well as the other decentralized baselines benefit from the full observations as you propose. The results are shown in appendix B2. Our methods outperforms all MARL baselines in terms of final reward and sample efficiency. It also approaches the performance of the centralized single agents, and even outperforms them in four-arm-lift.

**4- There are many other baselines that achieve better performance than SAC in robosuite, e.g., modular RL or any other algorithms that are cited in robosuite's documentation.**

First, we would like to point out that we also use SAC for training the agents of all MARL baselines as we mentioned in section 3.3, hence, the comparison to the single-agent baseline is fair. In addition, we looked into robosuite’s documentation and could only find SAC mentioned (same in the whitepaper). If you are referring to the use of an underlying controller to compute the joint torques, our baselines are all using the joint-velocity action space as the original action space. Using an underlying controller is a standard practice in robot reinforcement learning. We added these details in the setup section for further reproducibility.

**5- The results in Figure 7 are hard to understand. And this result is obtained from one seed, which might be not general.**

Figure 7 is meant to illustrate the potential action spaces that could be learned based on our method. It is hence purely a  qualitative result and is not meant to deliver any statements about our method. Like all qualitative results, it has to be drawn from one seed, since averaging over multiple seeds would make absolutely no sense (the latent space learned in each seed has a different meaning, and we show the one that is intuitively most interesting). To avoid confusion on this topic, we removed any hints or claims of interpretability from the whole paper and made it clear that is a qualitative result only.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the problem of multi-robot coordination in reinforcement learning and presents a method that learns a centralized latent action space which then is decoded to different decentralized agent actions. Experiments in customized simulation environments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms baselines, especially when scaling up with the number of agents and when there is disturbance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The idea of learning a central latent action by emphasizing the action’s effects on the object is neat, which offloads decentralized control to the action decoders, effectively reducing the multi-agent RL problem to single-agent learning. The proposed method also scales efficiently to more agents and is more robust to disturbances when compared with baseline fully decentralized or Q-based method.

For the model design, the authors did not discuss the distinction between latent state versus latent action. It seems the way the latent space is used, it could either represent state or action. If latent state is used, the decoders probably would no longer need the raw observations but would be forced to use the centralized information. It would be an interesting ablation to show a comparison of such and discuss the pros and cons of using a latent state vs a latent action space for shared control.

One weakness of this work is on the experiment end. The experimental environments are heavily customized, limited to a single type of task and use the same robot arms as decentralized agents; the optimal policy in these environments is also symmetric. It is unclear if CLAS could support learning in tasks where the agents have very different action spaces. At the same time it seems the only task CLAS has an advantage over baselines is multi-agent lifting. Is this task representative of all multi-agent manipulation tasks?

The paper is written with clarity and provides details.
The novelty is fair. The latent action idea has been explored in the centralized control idea and this work extends it to decentralized control.

content.title: Official Answer to Reviewer zCHf
content.comment:
Thank you for your positive feedback and insightful questions and for appreciating our ideas and work. Below we address your concerns:

**1– For the model design, the authors did not discuss the distinction between latent state versus latent action. It seems the way the latent space is used, it could either represent state or action. If latent state is used, the decoders probably would no longer need the raw observations but would be forced to use the centralized information. It would be an interesting ablation to show a comparison of such and discuss the pros and cons of using a latent state vs a latent action space for shared control.**

Indeed our model uses both observation and action as part of the inference and generation processes. However, it is important to note that the decoder only outputs actions and the loss is computed based on the log-likelihood of the actions and not observations. Hence, the latent space is supposed to encode action information with the help of the observations. Of course, this goal can be achieved without including the observations in the process. However, we decided to use this conditional VAE architecture because having state information helps learn more complex encoders and decoders capable of transformations such as the ones needed in (inverse) robot dynamics, where the state is necessary. The ablation you mentioned is very interesting in model-based methods where this latent action could also be used to predict future states/observations. However, this is beyond the scope of this paper, since it’s focused on model-free approaches.

**2- The experimental environments are heavily customized, limited to a single type of task and use the same robot arms as decentralized agents; the optimal policy in these environments is also symmetric. It is unclear if CLAS could support learning in tasks where the agents have very different action spaces**

That’s a very interesting question. As we’re also curious about this aspect, we performed the following experiment to validate it. We train our method as well as the baselines in the dual-arm-lift environment described before. However, this time we use a combination of a Sawyer robot whose agent works in an operational-space controller action space with a Panda robot equipped with the joint velocity action space. This way we break the symmetry you mentioned. The results are very interesting and can be seen in appendix B4. CLAS is the only decentralized method that finds policies capable of lifting the pot, while the other two decentralized baselines as well as SINGLE struggle to do so.

**3-  At the same time it seems the only task CLAS has an advantage over baselines is multi-agent lifting. Is this task representative of all multi-agent manipulation tasks?**

Multi-agent lifting has a lot of properties and requirements that are common to multi-agent manipulation problems such as the effect of the object dynamics on the control, and the need for coordination and estimation of the other agents' current and future actions. We don’t and wouldn’t claim that it is representative of all multi-agent manipulation tasks. In fact, we are not even sure that there exists a set of tasks that is representative of all multi-agent manipulation tasks. However, we believe that multi-agent lifting is the ideal environment to study the coordination of multiple robots in manipulation tasks, which is the main focus of this work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper takes the perspective of Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to coordinate multiple robots in table-top manipulation tasks. Rather than dealing with the size of the state-action space for centralized control, the approach adopts a more complex DEC-POMDP setup, which uses function approximation and variational inference to add an inductive bias to shaping a latent action space. Empirical results are presented based upon virtual domains, and the proposed method meets or exceeds the performance of baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
*The literature review does a good job to have a sentence or two at the end of each subsection in which the authors attempt to differentiate this work from prior work.
* The proposed DEC-POMDP method (CLAS) meets are exceeds the performance of centralized methods in three domains.
* The paper includes a sensitivity analysis to see how well the proposed method performs when disturbances are applied. The method appears to outperform baselines.


Weaknesses:
*The first paragraph ignores a lot of prior work in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). For starters, see: Zhang, K., Yang, Z. and Başar, T., 2021. Multi-agent reinforcement learning: A selective overview of theories and algorithms. Handbook of Reinforcement Learning and Control, pp.321-384.
*The paper says that solving multi-robot manipulation with RL results in a "combinatorial explosion." However, casting this problem as a centralized MDP results only in P-complete complexity whereas the proposed DEC-POMDP result is NEXP-complete, as the paper notes. As such, saying the DEC-POMDP approach is adopted because the MDP version has a "combinatorial explosion" does not quite make sense.
* The variational approach is interesting, but the paper is missing an explicit connection between Equation (2) and the RL approach (using SAC). Currently, Equation 2 appears to be a supervised learning loss function to learn a latent space rather than a policy. Section 3.3 does not elucidate the missing details.
*"physical tasks such as dual-arm manipulation" -- add a comma before "such"
*Formatting for citations is incorrect. For example: "such as in (Guestrin et al., 2002"
*This phrase should include citations: "policy architecture or the learning algorithm."
*Technically, a "multi-layer perceptron" is a neural network with multiple layers where the activations are perceptrons. Is this what the authors mean?
*The claim that "Next, we analyze the results from MARL-based methods. FULL DEC and SHARED Q struggle to keep up with single-agent RL methods. This indicates that our environments are well-suited for studying Dec-POMDPs, since they require a certain degree of coordination to be solved" is understandable but a bit strong. It could also be that the FULL DEC and SHARED Q methods are not well-designed for the problem.
* Figure 7 is not intuitive (also missing vertical axis labels). It would be helpful if the "interpreting the central latent action space" section could be re-thought.
* Along those lines, this paper does not provide interpretability in the typical sense, and it would be helpful if the paper did not make such claims. Please see: Rudin, C., Chen, C., Chen, Z., Huang, H., Semenova, L. and Zhong, C., 2022. Interpretable machine learning: Fundamental principles and 10 grand challenges. Statistics Surveys, 16, pp.1-85.
* How well would a basic, control-theoretic solution (traditional IK-based approaches/planners) work for solving these tasks?
* The paper does not appear to include code for reproducibility

The paper is missing key details to explain how the latent space is informed by and connected to RL.

The results section (particularly the interpretability results) are not intuitive.

Sukhbaatar, S. and Fergus, R., 2016. Learning multiagent communication with backpropagation. Advances in neural information processing systems, 29.

content.title: Official Answer to Reviewer pBfr: Part 1
content.comment:
We would like to thank you for the very thorough and constructive feedback. Your review helped substantially improve our paper. Below we address your concerns:

**1- The first paragraph ignores a lot of prior work in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). For starters, see: Zhang, K., Yang, Z. and Başar, T., 2021. Multi-agent reinforcement learning: A selective overview of theories and algorithms. Handbook of Reinforcement Learning and Control, pp.321-384.**

Thanks for pointing that out. In our previous “related work” section, we tried to limit ourselves to methods we felt are most relevant to our work, in that they either work with cooperative systems, DEC-POMDPS, or have ideas that can be transferred to such domains, especially for the application of multi-robot manipulation, which requires continuous actions. However, you are absolutely right. This section does ignore some seminal work in cooperative MARL. Hence, we updated our related work section on MARL methods. If you still think some prior work is missing, please feel free to either point us to the papers or at least the family of methods you believe should be mentioned. We will make sure to integrate them into the manuscript.

**2- The paper says that solving multi-robot manipulation with RL results in a "combinatorial explosion." However, casting this problem as a centralized MDP results only in P-complete complexity whereas the proposed DEC-POMDP result is NEXP-complete, as the paper notes. As such, saying the DEC-POMDP approach is adopted because the MDP version has a "combinatorial explosion" does not quite make sense.**

That’s a great point. Indeed DEC-POMDPs are more complex to solve than MDPs. However, in high-dimensional continuous action and state space domains, function approximations are needed to find solutions to these problems. The “combinatorial explosion” we refer to is not for solving the problems, but for the exploration and learning of the actor and/or critic networks needed to solve the problems.

**3- The variational approach is interesting, but the paper is missing an explicit connection between Equation (2) and the RL approach (using SAC). Currently, Equation 2 appears to be a supervised learning loss function to learn a latent space rather than a policy. Section 3.3 does not elucidate the missing details.**

The decoders learned in equation (2) are used to decode the outputs of the different agents policies. In the case where all agents share the same observation, they would then all have a copy of the same policy but different decoders learned via equation (2) this is shown in figure 2. In the case of partial observability, each agent would have its own policy as well as a copy of a common policy conditioned on the object observations. The concatenation of both policies outputs is then decoded by each agent's decoder to obtain an action in the native action space of the robot. We moved the graphical models to the appendix and replaced them with system figures so that we could introduce the overall approach in the beginning of section 3.2.


**4- "physical tasks such as dual-arm manipulation" -- add a comma before "such" Formatting for citations is incorrect. For example: such as in (Guestrin et al., 2002". This phrase should include citations: "policy architecture or the learning algorithm." Technically, a "multi-layer perceptron" is a neural network with multiple layers where the activations are perceptrons. Is this what the authors mean?**

We fixed the punctuation and formatting for citations and replaced the term with “multi-layer neural networks”.

content.comment:
**5- The claim that "Next, we analyze the results from MARL-based methods. FULL DEC and SHARED Q struggle to keep up with single-agent RL methods. This indicates that our environments are well-suited for studying Dec-POMDPs, since they require a certain degree of coordination to be solved" is understandable but a bit strong. It could also be that the FULL DEC and SHARED Q methods are not well-designed for the problem.**

We agree with your last statement “It could also be that the FULL DEC and SHARED Q methods are not well-designed for the problem.” However, this is the reason why we believe that this finding indicates our environments are well-suited for studying coordination since these two baselines do not explicitly encourage it. You are however right that our statement is a bit strong, hence we tone it down as you can see in the newer version of the paper. 

**6- Figure 7 is not intuitive (also missing vertical axis labels). It would be helpful if the "interpreting the central latent action space" section could be re-thought.
Along those lines, this paper does not provide interpretability in the typical sense, and it would be helpful if the paper did not make such claims. Please see: Rudin, C., Chen, C., Chen, Z., Huang, H., Semenova, L. and Zhong, C., 2022. Interpretable machine learning: Fundamental principles and 10 grand challenges. Statistics Surveys, 16, pp.1-85.**

Figure 7 is meant to be a qualitative analysis of the learned central latent action spaces. Hence we plot them for an interval of time, and first show how some of them are active while other dimensions which are not needed for the problem are just collapsed by the autoencoder. In the figure on the right, we show how one of the latent action trajectories highly correlates with the trajectory of the z-position of the pot which is the task object. In fact, the latent trajectory is ahead of the z-pot position, hence this learned latent action is the desired z-position of the pot. As you correctly say, this is not evidence of interpretability but just a qualitative result. Hence, we removed all hints of such claims to avoid reader confusion. We sincerely appreciate you pointing that out. We also added a vertical axis label to the figure.

**7- How well would a basic, control-theoretic solution (traditional IK-based approaches/planners) work for solving these tasks?**

Control–theoretic approaches could work reasonably well in the case where the object is rigidly attached to the end-effectors and its physical properties (such as mass and Inertia) are known. In that case, the object becomes part of the kinematic chain and the control is as usual. However, anytime these conditions are broken (e.g. our lifting environment, where the object is non-rigidly attached to the end-effectors and its properties unknown to the agents), a classical approach would require a lot of additional engineering efforts to solve such tasks. We added these details to the last paragraph of the introduction.

content.title: Official Answer to Reviewer JWTm
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback and time reviewing our work. Below we address your concerns:

**1- The problem is posed as decentralized POMDP, extending the work of Zhou et al. and Allshire et al. to a multi-agent setting. There is a lot of emphasis on task space planning in the paper, which is already well-understood in robotics. The state of the agent would naturally correspond to the task variables. The novelty and the use case of the paper is somewhat blurred.**

Thanks for pointing that out. From a robotics perspective, task space control/planning refers to expressing the problem with respect to the entity/object being controlled. In practice, however, this often corresponds to fixing the object at the end-effector and treating it as an additional link of the robot. Planning and control is then rendered (almost) equivalent to end-effector control as you mention. If however the object is not rigidly attached to the end-effector, this problem becomes substantially harder to solve, since the kinematics and dynamics would be a lot harder to model. Also, the state of the agent/robot is no longer the same as the task variables. An example of such a task would be pushing, or in our case lifting with the object being non-rigidly attached to the end-effectors. The multi-robot scenario is even harder since this object would be interacting with multiple robots. Our work is focused on learning mappings from the original action space of the robots to such a task-space action space, and another mapping for the other way around. We then learn policies that act in this learned task space and map their outputs back to the original action space of the robot (e.g. joint velocity commands) based on the learned mapping. This in turn simplifies the process of action generation by the policies which are decentralized due to the multi-robot setup. We hope the new version of this paper makes this contribution clearer. We also added system figures to section 3, which illustrate the overall concept.

**2- It would be helpful to define state variables explicitly in the experiments, in particular what is O_c. A comment on how this observation would be estimated in real experiments is also useful.**

That’s a great suggestion, we updated the setup section to contain this information. The majority of the common observations correspond to positions and orientations of the object being manipulated (peg, hole, pot) and the distance of the end-effector to them. 
In a real experiment such observations could either be obtained via some motion capture system or vision. The latter is rather challenging to establish, but it is also possible to learn a latent representation which contains the information that is shared across different views.

**3- The experimental setup consists of simple manipulation tasks that do not necessarily require complex state representations. For example, It would be particularly helpful to comment on how this approach would scale to visual robotic manipulation.**

Indeed, our environments do not require complex state representation. We intentionally chose such environments to make the experimental study and comparison more comprehensive and fair. Our focus is on learning action and not state representations. If we used environments that require state representation learning, evaluating our method would be tricky and potentially unfair since it would then be hard to disambiguate the effects of the state and action representation modules, which would ideally interact with one another.

Visual robotics manipulation is a very exciting area for us and this work. Theoretically, having a visual manipulation environment shouldn’t affect our method which is concerned with the action side of things. However, this area offers a lot of potential in jointly learning state and action representations that interact with each other and potentially adhere to joint constraints and inductive biases.

**4- The more interesting aspects of the multi-robot manipulation formulation are in cooperative and/or adversarial behaviors. Authors are encouraged to further investigate policy learning in handling complex manipulation tasks.**

Indeed we limited our experiments to only cooperative tasks. The choice of tasks was also dependent on the availability of open-source standardized environments which require multiple robots, we even built an additional environment (four-arm-lift) to test the scalability of our method to more than 2 robots which to our knowledge is not offered in any benchmark.

**5- The writing quality and representation of the paper could be further improved**

Thanks for pointing that out, we re-wrote a large part of the paper based on the reviewers' recommendations.

content.title: Common Answer
content.comment:
We would like to thank all reviewers for their feedback and recommendations on our work. Overall there haven’t been concerns about the technical details/correctness of the work, its central claims, or the experimental validation of the claims. In the following, we summarize changes we made to the paper based on common reviewers’ feedback.

**Literature Review** (reviewers ​​pBfr and pxRk)

We updated our “related work” section to include more diverse prior work on multi-agent RL (based on the requests by reviewer ​​pBfr) as well as action abstractions and representations (based on the request by reviewer pxRk). 

**Contribution and Novelty** (reviewers JWTm and pBfr)

Our work is concerned with learning multi-robot manipulation skills. On the one hand, treating the problem as a single-agent RL problem leads to high exploration and sample requirements. On the other hand, multi-agent RL solutions lack the coordination needed for such tasks. Hence, we propose to learn a centralized latent action space using variational inference and make the agents learn their decentralized policies in this centralized action space. Our experiments empirically demonstrate that this approach results in improved coordination.

We improved the writing of our first three sections in a way that better highlights our contributions and distinguishes our work from prior work. We replaced the graphical models with system figures, which in turn allowed us to first introduce our overall approach on an intuitive level.

**Interpretability** (reviewers pBfr and pxRk)

As reviewer pBfr points out, our results on interpreting the latent action space are different from the traditional sense of ML interpretability. These results are only qualitative and are meant to illustrate the potential action spaces that could be learned with our approach. Hence, we removed and toned down all hints of interpretability to avoid reader confusion.

**Additional Ablations** (reviewers pxRk and zCHf)

We performed additional experiments based on certain reviewers' concerns/questions:

- We demonstrate how our results are also valid under multi-agent systems with individual agents having full observability in comparison to our original results which assumed they have partial observability. The results are in appendix B2.
- We demonstrate the efficacy of our method in a non–symmetric environment, where the different agents handle different robots with different original action spaces. The results are in appendix B4.
